actTitle: Count the questions, then answer them
actSpeakBrief: Answer both halves aloud, and keep them the same length.
actSpeak1: Why do fewer young people learn to drive than twenty years ago — and is that a good thing? Two answers, one minute each.
actSpeak2: Your partner gives you a cause that is really just the trend reworded. Catch it, and push them for the mechanism underneath.
actSpeak3: Take a verdict you hold strongly. State its strongest objection first, at full strength, and then answer it.
actWriteBrief: In many countries, people are having children much later in life than they used to. Why is this happening, and do you think it is a positive or a negative development? One paragraph per question, and answer both in the introduction first.
actPlaceholder: Introduction: reframe, name your causes, then give your verdict…

coverSub: The last of the five types — and a way to tell any of them apart in the thirty seconds before you start writing
s2Title: Two questions, and both are marked
s2A: A direct question prompt asks two separate things. Each gets its own body paragraph, and the two should come out roughly the same size.
s2B: The failure is almost always the same: the first question is answered at length, and the second gets two sentences at the end.
s2Note: The second question usually asks for a judgement — positive or negative, is it a problem, should it continue. That is where the marks for position live.
s3A: Question one is causal. It wants explanation, not opinion — and two causes explained beat five listed.
s3B: Question two is a judgement. "Both" is not an answer to it. Choose, and say what you weighed to get there.
s4A: Both answers are already here. The causes in six words, the judgement in one clause. The body paragraphs will now prove what has been claimed.
s4B: "On balance" signals a judgement that has costs attached, which is what stops it reading as a slogan.
s6A: Two causes, each traced to a mechanism. Not "people are more independent" — which is a description of the trend wearing the costume of an explanation — but money, and a specific stretch of years that did not use to exist.
s7A: The strongest objection is met first, at full strength. Then it is narrowed — the harm is real but concentrated in old age — and answered with a benefit the other side never counts. That is a judgement, not a preference.
s9A: Sentence one settles the cause; sentence two settles the judgement. Both questions are answered again, in order, in fifty words.
s9B: The last clause converts the objection into a recommendation — which is a stronger finish than repeating that the writer was right.
s10A: "People are more independent" is the trend, not its cause. It describes living alone in different words and calls that an explanation. Four reasons are named and not one is traced to anything — the paragraph is a list wearing the shape of an argument.
s11Title: And the second question gets this
s11A: Three sentences against the first question's six — and no judgement in any of them. "It depends on the person" answers nothing, and the conclusion spends half its length re-listing the causes instead.
s13A: Opinion. "To what extent do you agree or disagree?" One position, stated early, held to the end.
s13B: Discussion. "Discuss both views and give your own opinion." Both sides fairly, then your own.
s13C: Advantages and disadvantages. "Do the advantages outweigh…?" Both sides weighed, and a verdict on which is heavier. Without outweigh in the prompt, both sides are enough.
s14Title: And the two that come in halves
s14A: Problem and measure. "What problems… what measures?" Two halves, and every measure aimed at a problem you raised.
s14B: Direct question. Two questions, one paragraph each, roughly equal — and the second almost always wants a judgement.
s14Note: One habit covers all five: before writing, count the things the prompt obliges you to produce. Then count them again at the end.

x06a: An examiner reads the whole answer either way. Saving reading time is not a criterion and would not earn a mark if it were.
x06b: It has the opposite effect — it commits the writer, in the first sixty words, to proving two specific claims.
x06c: A promise made early is a structure. Each body paragraph now has one job, and the reader can see it being done.
x06d: Introductions are not scored for length, and this one is short. What it gains is direction, not size.
x06e: Say what you will argue, then argue it. The shape does half the work of coherence.
x09a: Nothing is being balanced out. The paragraph narrows the objection and then outweighs it — it does not sit between the two.
x09b: The essay committed itself in the introduction and never moves. Raising an objection is not the same as being undecided.
x09c: An unpopular verdict is not what is happening here, and popularity is not marked. What is marked is whether the verdict was tested.
x09d: A judgement that has already answered its strongest counter-argument is worth far more than one that never met it.
x09e: Meet the objection at full strength, then narrow it. Never pretend it is not there.
x13a: Half the task was set aside. Thin development lowers a band; leaving a question effectively unanswered caps one.
x13b: Undeveloped causes do hurt, but the causes at least attempt the question. The judgement never arrives at all.
x13c: They are not equivalent. One is a weak answer to a question; the other is the absence of an answer to a question.
x13d: Repetition in a conclusion is a minor fault by comparison, and it is a symptom of having nothing left to say.
x13e: Ask of every prompt: how many questions? Then check you have answered that many.
x16a: Two would be the two views on their own. The instruction adds a third obligation after the word “and”, which is the one most often dropped.
x16b: View one, view two, and a stated opinion of your own. Miss the third and the answer cannot reach band 6 for task response.
x16c: A judgement on which view is stronger is not required here — that is the outweigh type. This prompt asks for your opinion, not a comparison.
x16d: One would be an opinion essay, which this is not. The prompt supplies two named views and requires both to be discussed.
x16e: Count the obligations before you plan. Most lost marks are a missing obligation, not a missing word.
x17a: The instruction, not the topic, decides the type. Read the last sentence of the prompt twice.
x18a: On balance — a verdict with costs attached. It answers the question without pretending the other side is empty.
x18b: Cause — and ranking it as the most straightforward tells the reader a second one is coming, and that it is subtler.
